Performance outcome

The rider walks a race track with a purpose: mapping features, line options, braking and decision zones, risk areas and conditions, and leaves with a first plan they expect to change after practice.

Who it’s for

Competitive downhill and enduro riders, and anyone preparing for a race on an unfamiliar track.

Before this lesson

  • Elite Line Choice is recommended.

Why it matters

The track walk is the first and cheapest practice run. Riders who walk with a plan arrive at practice knowing what to test.

Technical model

Source check: d01 (video only: not yet watched). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

What to look for

Major features; line options and where they split and rejoin; braking and decision zones; places to pass (where racing allows); high-risk spots; and conditions such as wet roots, loose corners and ruts.

Map it

Mark these on a simple track map or notes: section by section, with questions to answer in practice.

A plan, not the final line

The map is a starting plan. Practice laps will change it; the walk tells the rider what to test first.

Team input

Where riders have support, the coach, mechanic and suspension technician each notice different things on a walk. At the top level, the process runs from track walk to practice laps to final setup tweaks, with rider feedback at the centre.

Physics & maths

Mapping a track

A track map is a data model: a sequence of sections, each with features, line options, and estimated speed and risk. Splitting a run into sections is also how timing works (see Practice Laps). Gradients from a topographic map or GPS track show where the track is steep, as rise over run.

A good Mathlete visual: a track profile (elevation against distance) with sections and features marked.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Walking without a plan, or only looking at the big features.Not knowing what to look for.Coach to supply
Treating the walk plan as final.Not leaving room to change after practice.Coach to supply
Not re-checking after weather or heavy practice changes the track.Assuming conditions stay the same.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
On foot, on a race track or a local track treated as one.
Focus
Produce a section map with features, lines, decision zones and questions.
Feedback
Compare the walk plan with what actually happened in practice laps.

Stop when

  • Follow event rules for walking the track (some tracks restrict access).

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Does the map cover every section?
  • Are line options and decision zones marked?
  • Are questions for practice listed?
  • How much did the plan change after practice, and why?

Ready to move on

  • The rider produces a usable track map and a list of practice questions.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 1: performance foundations. Theory, analysis and planning. Practice still depends on terrain and context.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
